entities.summary:
Cristóbal de Olid (died 1524) was a prominent, albeit short-lived, Spanish conquistador whose military prowess and eventual rebellion profoundly impacted the early European subjugation of Mesoamerica. A trusted lieutenant of Hernán Cortés, Olid’s significance lies in his swift campaigns that expanded Spanish control, his pivotal participation in the fall of Tenochtitlan, and ultimately, his dramatic defiance against Cortés, which underscored the fierce rivalries and precarious authority within the nascent Spanish colonial enterprise. His actions directly contributed to the geopolitical reshaping of the Caribbean and Central American regions during the early 16th century.

Olid arrived in the New World in 1515, initially serving under Diego Velázquez in Cuba before joining Cortés's expedition to Mexico in 1519. He distinguished himself in key engagements against the Tlaxcalans and during the Noche Triste retreat in 1520, where he commanded a vital rearguard action. Following the siege and fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521, Olid led expeditions into Michoacán and Jalisco, extending Spanish dominion and securing resources. His most significant independent command came in 1523 when Cortés dispatched him with five ships and 400 soldiers to establish a colony in Honduras, a region coveted for its potential gold and strategic location.
